title: Rethinking Popularity Bias in Collaborative Filtering via Analytical Vector Decomposition

problem.claim: Popularity bias in collaborative filtering causes models to over-recommend popular items and neglect users' preferences for niche content.

gap.claim: Existing approaches treat popularity bias as an external confounding factor, while the paper identifies it as an intrinsic geometric artifact of BPR optimization.

contributions.claim: The paper mathematically analyzes BPR optimization and shows that it organizes item embeddings along a dominant popularity direction correlated with interaction frequency.
The paper proposes Directional Decomposition and Correction, a framework using asymmetric directional updates to correct popularity-related embedding geometry.
The paper explains how popularity-related geometry forces user embeddings to jointly represent genuine preference and calibrate against global popularity.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across multiple BPR-based architectures, the authors report that DDC outperforms state-of-the-art debiasing methods.
The authors report that DDC reduces training loss to less than 5% of heavily tuned baselines while achieving superior recommendation quality and fairness.
The authors report that code is available in a public GitHub repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: Popularity bias undermines personalization by favoring popular items over niche preferences.
The paper reframes popularity bias as an intrinsic geometric artifact of BPR optimization rather than an external confounder.
Mathematical analysis identifies a dominant popularity direction in item embeddings and conflicting demands on user embeddings.
DDC applies asymmetric directional updates to separate personalized preference directions from the global popularity direction.
Experiments on multiple BPR-based architectures report improvements over debiasing baselines in loss, recommendation quality, and fairness.

source_observation.claim: Popularity bias is described as an embedding-geometry problem tied to BPR optimization.

interpretation.claim: Diagnosing the geometric source of a bias may reveal a more direct intervention point than treating the bias only as an external nuisance.

application.claim: For optimization-induced recommendation bias, inspect learned representation directions and design updates that separate task-relevant preference from global frequency signals.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the proposed geometric diagnosis applies beyond BPR-based collaborative filtering architectures.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, evaluation metrics, or exact BPR-based architectures used.
The abstract does not provide proof details or assumptions underlying the mathematical analysis.
The abstract does not describe limitations, ablations, or independent verification of the reported results.
